faq.a: It is our home galaxy, a huge spiral of 100 to 400 billion stars, including the Sun, held together by gravity. Its name comes from the milky band of light it makes across the night sky.
asks: Is the Milky Way a galaxy?

faq.q: Where is the Sun in the Milky Way?
faq.a: About 26,000 light years from the centre, roughly halfway out, in a smaller spiral arm called the Orion Arm. The Sun takes about 230 million years to go round the galaxy once.
asks: How long does the Sun take to go round the galaxy?

faq.q: Why are there dark patches in the Milky Way?
faq.a: They are huge clouds of dust between the stars, blocking the light of the stars behind them. New stars are born inside such clouds.
asks: What is the dark rift in the Milky Way?

faq.q: Why can't I see the Milky Way from a city?
faq.a: Street lights and buildings brighten the sky, drowning out the Milky Way's faint glow. It is hidden from more than a third of people on Earth by light pollution.
asks: Where can I see the Milky Way?

faq.q: Where is the centre of the Milky Way?
faq.a: It lies in the direction of the constellation Sagittarius, where the band looks brightest and thickest. At the very centre is a giant black hole called Sagittarius A star, about 4 million times the mass of the Sun.
asks: Is there a black hole in the Milky Way?

facts: The Milky Way is about 100,000 light years across.
The Sun lies about 26,000 light years from the centre of the Milky Way.
Light pollution hides the Milky Way from more than a third of humanity (World Atlas of Artificial Night Sky Brightness, 2016).
